hints: Separate quantities defined independently in the SI system from quantities formed by combining other quantities.
walkthrough: The SI base quantities include mass and electric current; each has its own base unit, kilogram and ampere respectively.
Energy is derived from work done and force is derived from mass and acceleration, so neither is an SI base quantity.

ai_rubric.observable: Ticks current and mass, with energy and force left unticked.

hints: Begin with power as a rate: identify the energy-transfer quantity and the time quantity in its definition.
Use joule as kg m² s⁻², then divide by the unit second and combine the time powers.
walkthrough: Power is work done, or energy transferred, per unit time: P = W / t.
Work done has the SI unit joule, J = kg m² s⁻².
Therefore the unit of power is J s⁻¹ = (kg m² s⁻²) / s.
Combining the time factors gives the SI base units kg m² s⁻³.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses power as work done or energy transferred divided by time.
Converts J s⁻¹ to the SI base units kg m² s⁻³.

hints: Intensity is power per unit area, so rearrange that relationship for the power reaching the sensor.
Convert the sensor area from cm² to m² before multiplying by the intensity in W m⁻².
walkthrough: For light incident normally on the sensor, the power received is intensity multiplied by sensor area: P = IA.
Substitute the intensity and area: P = 950 × 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ W.
This gives P = 0.209 W, which to two significant figures is 0.21 W.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses P = IA, or an equivalent rearrangement of intensity as power per area.
Converts the sensor area to 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ m² and substitutes it with the stated intensity.
Obtains the power of the incident daylight as 0.21 W.
